claims.claim: Emergency preparedness is the knowledge and capacities and organizational systems built before emergencies so that governments, response and recovery organizations, communities, and individuals can anticipate, respond to, and recover from them.

The emergency cycle has four phases — prevent, prepare, respond, recover — and the WHO Health EDRM Framework emphasizes prevention, preparedness and readiness together with response and recovery to save lives and protect health.

The U.S. federal government frames preparedness through five mission areas — prevention, protection, mitigation, response, recovery — per FEMA's National Preparedness framework (PPD-8), and treats preparedness as a shared whole-community responsibility.

Preparedness plans for families of threats — outbreaks, natural disasters, and chemical events — because the underlying systems overlap; FEMA plans capabilities against all threats and hazards (earthquakes, chemical spills, pandemics), and MedlinePlus organizes disaster topics into natural disasters, chemical emergencies, and biodefense categories.

Surveillance is a core preparedness system: the International Health Regulations (2005) require countries to establish and maintain core capacities for surveillance and response and to notify WHO of public health risks and events with actual or potential international implications.

Stockpiling is a standard preparedness activity — the UN disaster-risk terminology names 'the stockpiling of equipment and supplies' as preparedness work — and in the United States the Strategic National Stockpile, managed by HHS's ASPR, holds national reserves of medical countermeasures and supplies.

Deployable response teams are part of preparedness: the U.S. National Disaster Medical System (ASPR) provides trained medical teams that respond in disasters, and WHO coordinates a global network of emergency operations centres.

Communication plans are a named preparedness system: WHO lists communicating risk in public health emergencies among its core work, and the UN terminology includes arrangements for public information among preparedness activities.

CDC's readiness programs support state and local health departments — the Division of State and Local Readiness works on public health emergency preparedness and response capabilities, including the Cities Readiness Initiative.

Preparedness is inherently unglamorous: its success conditions are unused stockpiles and uneventful drills, and the WHO Framework notes that not all emergencies can be predicted but they can be prepared for.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many phases the emergency management cycle has
positions: Public-health teaching and the WHO Health EDRM Framework use four phases: prevention, preparedness, response, recovery.
The U.S. federal government's National Preparedness Goal uses five mission areas: prevention, protection, mitigation, response, recovery.
Some models use three phases (preparedness, response, recovery) or add readiness as a distinct stage.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the four-phase health cycle (prevent, prepare, respond, recover) as the working model, names the U.S. federal five-mission framing in one line for context, and does not claim a single universal list.

sourceRecords.title: International Health Regulations (Health Topics)
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: the IHR (2005) provide an overarching legal framework defining countries' rights and obligations for public health risks and events with potential to cross borders; they are legally binding on 197 countries; countries must establish and maintain core capacities for surveillance and response (including at points of entry) and notify WHO of public health risks or events with actual or potential international implications. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: What we do — WHO Health Emergencies Programme
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports the phase framing: 'From prevention through preparedness to early warning, response, and early recovery, the WHO Health Emergencies programme is operational'; the work areas 'Strengthening readiness to respond to emergencies' and 'Communicating risk in public health emergencies'; and 'Coordinating a global network of emergency operations centres.' Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Health Emergency and Disaster Risk Management Framework (2019)
sourceRecords.notes: Read the WHO publications item page (Director-General's foreword) directly 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). The foreword states the Framework 'emphasizes the critical importance of prevention, preparedness and readiness, together with response and recovery, to save lives and protect health'; that emergencies range from cyclones and drought to major outbreaks and more localized events; and 'Not all emergencies can be predicted, but they can be prepared for.' Used for the phase framing and the ethos of preparedness. The full PDF is served through a JS-only IRIS viewer and could not be retrieved programmatically, so no claim relies on text beyond the verified foreword.

sourceRecords.title: Sendai Framework Terminology on Disaster Risk Reduction: Preparedness
sourceRecords.provider: United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR)
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Verified verbatim the UN definition: 'The knowledge and capacities developed by governments, response and recovery organizations, communities and individuals to effectively anticipate, respond to and recover from the impacts of likely, imminent or current disasters,' and the annotation naming contingency planning, the stockpiling of equipment and supplies, arrangements for coordination/evacuation/public information, and training and field exercises as preparedness activities. The WHO health-emergency version adapts this definition to health emergencies; the lesson attributes the definition family to the WHO/UN working definition. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: National Preparedness
sourceRecords.notes: fema.gov blocks direct fetch (HTTP 403); read 2026-08-22 via an Internet Archive capture (web.archive.org/web/20240809071727/https://www.fema.gov/emergency-managers/national-preparedness). Supports: FEMA develops capabilities needed to 'prevent, protect against, respond to, recover from, and mitigate against all threats and hazards,' with risks ranging from earthquakes and cyberattacks to chemical spills and pandemics; Presidential Policy Directive 8 recognizes preparedness as a shared responsibility of the whole community; the five mission areas (Prevention, Protection, Mitigation, Response, Recovery). Canonical URL recorded; no wording reproduced.
